title: Database Mirroring
description: Understand database mirroring concepts, operating modes, and how to implement disaster recovery in SQL Server.

data.text: Database mirroring is a legacy high-availability technology that maintains a hot standby copy of a database on a separate server instance. Every transaction committed on the principal database is sent to the mirror database, which replays the log in near real time. Although database mirroring has been deprecated in favor of Always On Availability Groups, it remains relevant for understanding SQL Server HADR evolution and for legacy environments that have not yet migrated.

data.title: Deprecated but Not Gone
data.text: Microsoft deprecated database mirroring in SQL Server 2012 and recommends migrating to Always On Availability Groups. However, mirroring still works in current versions, and many production systems rely on it. Knowing mirroring is valuable for maintaining legacy systems and for interviews.

items: Principal: The read-write database instance that accepts client connections and transactions.
Mirror: The hot standby instance that continuously applies transaction log records from the principal.
Witness: An optional third instance that enables automatic failover by providing an additional vote to establish quorum.

data.text: Database mirroring supports three operating modes that trade off safety, performance, and automation. High Safety (synchronous) mode ensures the mirror commits before the principal acknowledges the transaction. High Performance (asynchronous) mode removes the latency penalty by acknowledging immediately after the principal commits. High Safety with Witness adds a witness server to enable automatic failover because the witness provides the third vote needed for quorum.

data.caption: Database mirroring operating modes and failover behavior
data.definition:
graph LR
    subgraph Mode1[High Safety - Synchronous]
        P1[Principal] -->|log records| M1[Mirror]
        P1 -.->|commit wait| M1
        W1[Witness] -.->|vote| P1
    end
    subgraph Mode2[High Performance - Asynchronous]
        P2[Principal] -->|log records| M2[Mirror]
        P2 -.->|no wait| M2
    end
    subgraph Mode3[High Safety with Witness]
        P3[Principal] -->|log records| M3[Mirror]
        W3[Witness] -.->|vote| P3
        W3 -.->|vote| M3
    end

data.title: Data Loss Risk
data.text: In high-performance (asynchronous) mode, failover can result in data loss because uncommitted transactions on the principal may not have been sent to the mirror. Use FORCE_SERVICE_ALLOW_DATA_LOSS only as a last resort when the principal is unrecoverable.

data.title: Query mirroring status with sys.database_mirroring
data.content: Returns the mirroring state, safety level, and witness status for each mirrored database.
data.code:
SELECT
    d.name AS DatabaseName,
    m.mirroring_state_desc,
    m.mirroring_safety_level_desc,
    m.mirroring_witness_state_desc,
    m.log_send_queue_size,
    m.redo_queue_size,
    m.mirroring_failover_lsn
FROM sys.database_mirroring m
JOIN sys.databases d ON m.database_id = d.database_id
WHERE m.mirroring_state IS NOT NULL;

data.title: Database Mirroring Key Points
points: Database mirroring maintains a hot standby copy of a principal database on a mirror instance.
High Safety (synchronous) mode prevents data loss but adds latency.
High Performance (asynchronous) mode minimizes latency but may lose data on failover.
A witness server enables automatic failover by providing quorum.
Database mirroring is deprecated; prefer Always On Availability Groups for new deployments.
data.takeaway: Database mirroring is a straightforward disaster-recovery technology that teaches core HADR concepts such as log shipping, quorum, and failover modes. Understanding mirroring makes it easier to evaluate whether Always On AGs are the right upgrade path for a legacy environment.
